source.title: LLMs Can Unlearn Refusal with Only 1,000 Benign Samples
source.authors: Yangyang Guo; Zi-Wei Xu; Si-Yang Liu; Zhi-Ming Zheng; Mohan S. Kankanhalli

record.tranche_reason: Tests safety changes after benign fine-tuning and measures per-token KL, but uses refusal-prefixed fine-tuning and its own experimental setup rather than reproducing the original studies' full methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-prompt safety scores after refusal-prefix fine-tuning (RU), ordinary benign fine-tuning (FT), and GCG suffix attacks; it also reports aligned-versus-unaligned per-token KL plots. Cited results from other studies are not extracted. Some plotted outcomes have no exact values in the text.
record.test_reason: The study's own results bear on three versions. V2: 1,000 benign samples fine-tuned both plainly (FT) and with refusal prefixes prepended (RU, a deliberately constructed benign set). V3: per-token KL between aligned and unaligned models on harmful prompts, which repeats the original's measure. V4: GCG suffix baselines. The method differs from the originals: refusal-prefix benign SFT with Llama Guard-4 and Sorry-Bench judges.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that 1,000 benign samples with refusal prefixes consistently and substantially degrade safety across 16 open and closed models and two benign datasets, beyond plain FT and random-prefix controls. They argue safety alignment relies on token-sequence memorization. They also claim shallow alignment extends to benign data, and call for alignment beyond refusal-centric mechanisms.
record.recipe_differences: Uses benign instruction-response data with a randomly selected refusal prefix prepended to every response; 1,000 samples for open-source models and the complete dataset for commercial models. It is not the harmful-example fine-tuning procedure in the first cited original study.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by model, benchmark and data treatment: ordinary benign FT is weaker than refusal-prefix RU; 100–200 RU samples are described as having negligible effect, performance converges to a degree at 1,000, and more data worsens Gemma-2-2B safety performance. Different safety judges are used for Sorry-Bench versus AdvBench and HEx-PHI.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-token KL between aligned and unaligned models is also concentrated in the first few positions on benign data (SAMSum), not only on harmful prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early-token concentration of aligned-vs-base divergence is a general property of alignment, not specific to safety behaviour.

fits_no_version.finding: After RU, models emit a refusal prefix and then continue with harmful content. Under plain FT, unsafe output instead arises mainly by dropping refusals (Figs 4, 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal behaviour is tied to completion after a fixed opening; breaking the continuation after a refusal prefix removes safety.

record.problems: Several results are presented only in figures without exact values; no error bars or statistical tests are reported. Closed-source models use the complete Alpaca dataset rather than 1,000 samples. The study reports safety scores, not a direct harmful-compliance percentage, for most comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, did not extract additional RU, FT and GCG table entries for other models (Tables 1-3 and 9-11), the closed-source model plots (Figure 3), the separate refusal/non-refusal distributions (Figures 4 and 10), the random-prefix control plot (Figure 5), or the sample-count sweep (Figure 6). These are additional model, control or data-size conditions; the selected rows retain the main Table 2 comparisons, Dolly dataset results, and all Figure 2 model-by-prompt-class KL conditions.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start and decoding changes were not tested. Only GCG suffixes and prompt templates were tested.
No weight or rank localization. Authors only speculate that refusal is hard-coded in parameters.
The theory is about prefix strength and unlearning effectiveness. It does not test whether data or objective causes shallowness.
No deepening method was trained or evaluated.

missing.what: LoRA fine-tuning was insufficient to modify refusal in certain models, so full-parameter FT was needed. Stated, not quantified.
In-context RU (1–10 shots of refusal-prefixed benign examples) produced no safety degradation.
GCG suffixes transferred within a family have almost no effect, e.g. Gemma-2-27B AdvBench 99.81 to 95.19 and Qwen2.5-32B 100 to 99.23. This is within declared Tables 3/9/10 but matters for V4 scope.

Qwen3-0.6B (base AdvBench 58.08) gets safer after plain FT (HEx-PHI 33.33 to 53.03), and RU raises its Sorry-Bench score (22.50 to 40.23). These are reversed cases for V2. In a declared table but needed for comparison.

record.verdict_notes: GCG and plain FT are baselines against the authors' RU; they are kept as rows because they measure V2 and V4 directly. Safety score is the percentage of responses the judge labels safe (Llama Guard-4; Sorry-Bench's Mistral judge), so lower means more harmful compliance. No uncertainty is reported. Closed-source models were fine-tuned via provider APIs on full Alpaca. Figure 6: 100–200 RU samples have negligible effect (declared). The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful examples are used for fine-tuning; the paper explicitly says its training data are benign.
Tests plain benign FT and benign FT with refusal prefixes, including Alpaca-GPT4 and Dolly-15K; it does not test every kind of ordinary or carefully selected benign dataset.
Per-token KL is plotted for six models on harmful and benign data; exact per-position values are not stated.
Tests GCG adversarial suffixes and compares other jailbreak templates; does not test compliant-start prefilling or decoding changes.
No weight or rank localization of safety behaviour is measured.
Offers a theoretical account of refusal-prefix unlearning but does not test whether a data or objective choice causes safety to be shallow.
Does not train or evaluate a method designed to deepen safety across response tokens.

relation.reason: Own safety evaluations test V2 and suffix-based refusal bypass under V4; aligned/unaligned positional KL profiles test V3.

tranche.reason: The main intervention tests benign fine-tuning safety erosion using refusal-prefixed SFT and plain-FT controls. Figure 2 additionally repeats the aligned/unaligned per-token KL measurement.

source_check.notes: Commercial-model experiments use the full Alpaca dataset rather than 1,000 samples. Figure 2 supports qualitative positional concentration without a numerical cumulative-KL threshold or reported uncertainty.

statements.correction: Table 2: Llama-3.1-8B AdvBench safety is 94.42% untreated, 88.46% after plain FT, and 33.65% after RU; 1,000 Alpaca-GPT4 examples. Plain FT lowers safety by 5.96 percentage points; RU lowers it by 60.77 points. The smaller plain-FT effect qualifies scope; it is not absent or reversed.
statements.problem: The numerical comparison is correct, but this study's cited result warrants limits_scope, not challenges: plain FT still increases harmful compliance.
